title: Hybrid tiered prefill-decode arbiter with opportunistic fast-paths and fairness budgets
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Background: current prefill/decode arbitrator favors strict token-based fairness and coarse timeout heuristics. That approach provides good long-term throughput but causes noticeable latency spikes for latency-sensitive customers during mixed workloads (short chat vs long-completion). Proposal: implement a hybrid, tiered arbiter that classifies incoming requests into latency tiers and applies an opportunistic fast-path plus a budgeted fairness mechanism to avoid starvation of high-cost requests. Goals: 1) reduce P50/P95 latency for tiered-latency requests by 20-30% without increasing cluster token cost by more than 5%; 2) prevent >1% increase in long-request tail (>1k tokens) completion time; 3) keep scheduler overhead CPU <3% of runtime process.
design_decision_summary: We will not pursue a pure priority queue because it leads to starvation. Instead, requests get a latency_tier label (L0: latency-sensitive, L1: balanced, L2: throughput/batch). Each tier receives an initial token budget per sliding window and a soft deadline. The arbiter grants prefill and decode slots preferentially to L0 up to budget, but allows opportunistic fast-paths: short-prefill fast-pass for requests whose estimated prefill tokens < X and expected decode length < Y. Long requests can be 'stealed-from' no more than Z tokens per window to satisfy L0 demands. The arbiter runs a lightweight scoring function: score = base_priority + urgency_boost - cost_penalty, with tunable coefficients. We will implement the arbiter as a runtime plugin to keep rollout safe and enable A/B tests.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Risk: extra context switches if the arbiter preempts decode streams too aggressively — mitigation: limit preemptions per-request and prefer cooperative handoffs.
Tradeoff: short-prefill fast-path improves latency but may reduce batching efficiency; mitigation: fast-path only for requests where batching benefit < threshold and when CPU headroom exists.
Risk: KV cache thrash from interleaving many small prefills and large decodes — mitigation: sticky allocation for active contexts and cache-aware scheduling heuristics.
Tradeoff: fairness budgets introduce complexity in debugging billing spikes — mitigation: dashboarding and per-tenant budget traces, plus opt-out per-customer flag.
Risk: incorrect token cost estimates leading to misclassification — mitigation: use conservative estimates from model profiles and runtime feedback loop to recalibrate.
implementation_notes: Componentization: 1) Classifier module (assigns latency_tier, estimates token cost) 2) Budget manager (sliding-window counters, per-tenant or per-route budgets) 3) Arbiter core (scoring + grant/steal logic) 4) Fast-path executor (short-prefill optimized flow) 5) Observability hooks (granular traces and budget metrics). We'll add feature flags and rollout gates: feature_flag.hybrid_arbiter and feature_flag.fastpath. Config surface: per-route latency_tier, budget_tokens_per_minute, steal_limit_per_window, fastpath_max_prefill, cost_coefficients. Implementation will live in runtime/arbiter plugin and expose a REST/Console page for threshold tuning.
experiment_plan: Phase 1 (prototype): implement classifier + budget manager + simple grant logic in sandbox container and run synthetic mixes (80/20 short/long, uniform, heavy-long). Compare with baseline scheduler. Phase 2 (dogfood): enable on internal tenants with feature flag for 5% of traffic; collect metrics for 2 weeks. Phase 3 (ramp): A/B test against baseline in region us-west-2 for 25% traffic for 1 week. Success criteria: latency-sensitive P95 reduced >=20% and no >5% regression in long-request P99. Rollback if budget_exhaustion_rate > 10% or customer complaints > threshold.
prototyping_results: Synthetic 80/20 short/long: P95 latency for L0 dropped 28% in prototype; average batch size decreased 12% leading to 3.7% token cost increase in microbenchmarks on A100-80GB nodes.
KV-cache miss rate rose initially by 0.9pp in worst-case mixes; adding sticky allocation reduced this to 0.2pp.
Scheduler CPU overhead measured at ~1.8% in prototype run at 5000 qps; acceptable for runtime-1.22 target.
Edge case: very-high-concurrency long-requests (>10k tokens) saw a small tail regression; we added 'long_request_protection' which reduces steal rate for requests flagged as important.
open_questions: What should the default per-tenant budget be for free-tier vs enterprise? (Cost/latency tradeoff)
How to expose enough observability to customers without leaking multi-tenant activity patterns?
Thresholds for fast-path (prefill token cutoff and decode length) need production-calibrated numbers across models/quantizations.
Should we allow customer-configurable policies that can opt out of being stolen-from? (enterprise customers might require guaranteed throughput)
Do we need additional kernel-level affinity hints for fast-path to reduce context-switch costs?
